strengths: Principled and novel formulation: Adapting noise schedules per instance according to radially-averaged power spectral density (RAPSD) is well-motivated by the spectral characteristics of natural images, offering a clear conceptual explanation for why conventional heuristics work across resolutions.

Sound theoretical derivation and clean closed forms: The derivation of bounds on minimum and maximum noise levels (Section 4.2) and the resulting closed-form expressions for the power-law parameterization (Appendix B) are elegant and mathematically rigorous.

Rigorous experimental validation: The authors compare against well-matched baselines (reproducing SiD2 with the identical architecture and training protocol) across three resolutions on ImageNet and text-to-image on MS-COCO. The method consistently achieves competitive or better FID with substantially fewer denoising steps (e.g., 160–256 vs. 512).

Comprehensive ablations and insightful control: Ablation studies effectively isolate the contribution of each design component (fixed median schedule, cosine min/max, separate frequency/power schedules, FiLM conditioning, guidance interval). Additionally, manipulating the sampled spectral parameters provides an intuitive, controllable mechanism for adjusting texture detail and contrast.

Thorough and transparent analysis of limitations: The authors explicitly analyze and investigate the FID degradation observed at high sampling step counts (Section C.1 and Table 4), demonstrating that it stems primarily from diversity loss and can be mitigated by adjusting inference noise injection.
weaknesses: Two-stage inference overhead: Although lightweight, generation requires training and sampling from an auxiliary model (the RAPSD GMM sampler) prior to running the reverse diffusion process, adding practical system complexity compared to standard fixed-schedule models.

Performance degradation at high NFE: The tight schedule can lead to performance degradation when the step count increases beyond an optimal threshold (e.g., at 512 steps in Figure 3), requiring careful selection of sampling step counts or adjustments to sampling hyperparameters like $\gamma$.

Scope limited to pixel-space diffusion: The approach is demonstrated solely for single-stage pixel diffusion models. While justified as a way to close the gap with latent diffusion models (LDMs), the method's applicability to latent spaces or rectified flow models remains unverified empirically.

strengths: Principled and well-motivated connection between natural image power spectral density (RAPSD) and diffusion noise schedules, providing a clear theoretical explanation for empirical resolution-dependent shifting heuristics used in prior pixel diffusion literature.
Derivation of explicit, interpretable bounds on minimum and maximum noise levels based on spectral properties, which effectively eliminates redundant denoising steps and produces 'tight' schedules.
Simple and computationally lightweight conditioning mechanism that models power-law parameters using a small Gaussian Mixture Model, introducing virtually zero inference overhead.

Solid empirical evaluation on ImageNet (128x128, 256x256, 512x512) and zero-shot MS-COCO text-to-image, consistently outperforming the competitive SiD2 baseline while requiring substantially fewer sampling steps (e.g., 160-256 vs. 512 NFE).

Thorough ablation studies and diagnostics examining schedule designs, conditioning inputs, timestep-based guidance intervals, high-NFE degradation, and controllable image editing via spectral parameter manipulation.
weaknesses: The methodology is strictly evaluated on and tailored to single-stage pixel diffusion; because latent representations exhibit very different spectral characteristics, applicability to latent diffusion models (LDMs) remains unverified.

While the minimum and maximum noise endpoints are theoretically grounded, the trajectory connecting them (the mixed schedule) relies on an empirical combination of frequency- and power-focused heuristics.

Tighter schedules suffer from sample degradation (primarily loss of recall/diversity) at higher denoising step counts, requiring careful selection of optimal NFE or tuning of the stochasticity parameter gamma.

Introduces several additional design choices and hyperparameters (such as kappa_min, kappa_max, GMM component count, and timestep-based CFG intervals) that must be managed alongside standard diffusion training.

strengths: Principled and well-motivated framework: Grounding per-instance noise schedules in the radially-averaged power spectral density (RAPSD) and the classic power-law decay of natural images provides a sound physical and theoretical motivation for defining tight noise bounds (kappa_min and kappa_max).

Rigorous and fair benchmarking: The empirical comparison against SiD2 is carefully controlled, utilizing identical architectures and training recipes. Across ImageNet resolutions (128x128, 256x256, 512x512) and zero-shot MS-COCO, the proposed schedule achieves competitive or superior FID/IS metrics while requiring substantially fewer sampling steps (e.g., 160–256 NFEs versus 512).

Comprehensive ablations and analysis: The manuscript thoroughly validates individual components, comparing the mixed schedule against frequency-only, power-only, fixed median, and cosine baselines, as well as ablating the extra FiLM conditioning and guidance interval parameterizations.

Controllability and interpretability: Parameterizing the schedule via the power-law parameters (alpha and beta) enables intuitive post-hoc control over high-frequency details and image contrast at test time without retraining the backbone.

Clear presentation and reproducibility: The mathematical derivations in the appendix are clear, algorithms are explicitly provided for both training and sampling, and implementation hyperparameters are fully detailed.
weaknesses: Performance degradation at high NFEs: As shown in Figure 3 and Table 4, image fidelity (FID) noticeably degrades when increasing sampling steps beyond an optimal threshold (e.g., on 128x128 flop heavy, FID degrades from 1.30 at 160 steps to 1.85 at 512 steps). While Appendix C.1 provides an analysis attributing this to diversity loss, it highlights an inherent brittleness/sensitivity in the tight scheduling compared to standard schedules that typically plateau or improve monotonically.

Moderate absolute improvements in the compute-heavy regime: On the most competitive models (flop heavy), the absolute FID improvements over SiD2 are modest (e.g., 1.45 vs. 1.48/1.53 at 512x512, and matching at 1.30 at 128x128). While the reduction in NFEs is beneficial, it still operates in the 160–320 NFE range, which remains substantially more expensive than modern distilled or latent diffusion models.

System and sampling complexity: Generating an image requires a two-stage inference procedure involving an auxiliary RAPSD sampler (GMM conditioned on prompt/label), along with architectural modifications to condition the network on schedule boundary values.

Restricted applicability to pixel-space models: The theoretical formulation relies fundamentally on the scale-free 1/f^alpha spectral characteristics of natural RGB pixels. As acknowledged by the authors, this does not readily translate to latent diffusion models (LDMs) where latent feature representations do not exhibit standard natural image Fourier statistics.

strengths: Principled and well-motivated framework: Grounding the diffusion noise schedule in the classical power-law spectral statistics of natural images ($1/f^\alpha$) provides an elegant theoretical justification that replaces empirical, resolution-dependent heuristic schedule shifting.

Rigorous formulation and closed-form solutions: The paper derives tight theoretical bounds for the minimum and maximum noise levels and provides closed-form expressions for both frequency-focused and power-focused schedules (and their mixture).

Solid empirical gains in pixel diffusion: Demonstrates consistent improvements across multiple ImageNet resolutions (128x128, 256x256, 512x512) over the direct baseline SiD2, cutting the required number of function evaluations (NFE) by approximately half while achieving better or comparable FID/IS.

Comprehensive ablations: Table 2 provides valuable insight into the necessity of mixing frequency- and power-focused schedules, per-instance vs. fixed median schedules, and conditioning mechanisms, confirming that the auxiliary RAPSD sampler incurs almost no performance penalty compared to the oracle ground-truth spectrum.

Controllability application: Showing that manipulating the sampled spectral slope $\alpha$ intuitively modulates the level of fine detail and texture in generated images (Figure 5) is a compelling practical byproduct.
weaknesses: Narrow domain of empirical validation: Experiments are restricted strictly to class-conditional ImageNet using a single architecture family (SiD2 U-ViT). Testing on text-to-image benchmarks (e.g., MS-COCO) or evaluating applicability to latent diffusion models (LDMs) would significantly strengthen the empirical claims regarding general applicability.

FID degradation at higher step counts: As seen in Figure 3, the proposed schedule experiences performance degradation as NFE increases past the optimal count (e.g., at 512 steps), in contrast to standard schedules which generally plateau. The paper highlights this phenomenon as interesting but offers little theoretical or empirical explanation.

Additional pipeline complexity: Introducing an auxiliary GMM-based RAPSD sampler and modifying conditioning to include minimum and maximum logSNR adds extra components and hyperparameter sensitivity (e.g., retuning classifier-free guidance intervals in $t$-space as shown in Table 4).

Diminishing returns at scale: In the compute-heavy model at 512x512, the improvement margin over the reproduced SiD2 baseline is relatively small (FID 1.45 vs. 1.53 reproduced / 1.48 original), suggesting that scaling model capacity may partially compensate for suboptimal schedules.

strengths: Principled spectral motivation: Connecting natural image radially-averaged power spectral density (RAPSD, following $k^\alpha$) to diffusion noise scheduling is an intuitive and conceptually appealing idea that grounds empirical schedule-shifting heuristics in analytical signal properties.

Closed-form derivations: The paper derives closed-form expressions for both frequency-focused and power-focused noise schedules (and their mixture) using the power-law parameterization, avoiding expensive numerical inversion during training.

Demonstrated step efficiency at low NFE: For single-stage pixel diffusion—which notoriously requires large step counts (e.g., 512 steps in SiD2)—the proposed schedule achieves competitive or superior FID at 160–256 steps, significantly improving sampling efficiency in that regime.

Controllable generation via spectrum editing: The ability to modulate texture and fine details post-training by scaling the sampled power-law exponent $\alpha$ (Figure 5) is an interesting and practical emergent capability of the instance-conditioned setup.
weaknesses: Performance degradation at higher step counts: As seen in Figure 3, the proposed schedule exhibits noticeable FID degradation at higher step counts (e.g., NFE = 512), where the SiD2 baseline continues to improve or remain stable. The manuscript notes this phenomenon but offers neither a theoretical explanation nor an empirical mitigation for why 'tight' schedules fail to scale gracefully with more inference budget.

Confounding gains from guidance and conditioning hyperparameter tuning: A substantial portion of the performance difference appears driven by tuning orthogonal components rather than the spectral schedule alone. Specifically, switching guidance intervals from logSNR to $t$-space contributes notably to performance (Table 2: FID drops from 1.58 to 1.42), and the guidance intervals require resolution-specific per-model tuning (Table 4 & Table 5). Additionally, without min/max conditioning, performance degrades to 1.58 FID.

Narrow experimental scope: Evaluation is confined exclusively to class-conditional ImageNet generation on top of a single base architecture/framework (SiD2). The method is not evaluated on text-to-image synthesis, nor on other common pixel-space generative benchmarks (e.g., FFHQ, CelebA-HQ, CIFAR-10), leaving its generalizability across diverse data distributions and modalities unverified.

Marginal performance gains on larger models: On the compute-heavy architectures, performance improvements over reproduced SiD2 are minimal (e.g., ImageNet 128x128 FLOP-heavy gets 1.30 vs. 1.26 baseline; ImageNet 512x512 FLOP-heavy gets 1.45 vs. 1.48 baseline), indicating that the advantage of per-instance scheduling diminishes as model capacity grows.

Added system complexity: The approach requires fitting power laws per batch image, training an external class-conditioned GMM sampler for the spectral parameters, and introducing extra conditioning paths into the diffusion backbone, which complicates an otherwise simple pixel diffusion training pipeline.

strengths: Principled and elegant formulation: Grounding diffusion noise schedules in the power spectral density (RAPSD) and the well-known 1/f power law of natural images provides a solid theoretical and physical justification for schedule design across resolutions.

Derivation of closed-form schedules: The paper neatly derives the expected RAPSD of perturbed images, establishes criteria for minimum and maximum noise levels, and derives closed-form formulas for frequency-focused, power-focused, and mixed schedules.

Solid empirical gains on single-stage pixel diffusion: On ImageNet class-conditional generation across 128x128, 256x256, and 512x512 resolutions, the proposed method consistently improves upon the SiD2 baseline while reducing required sampling steps (NFEs) significantly (e.g., from 512 down to 160-256).

Thorough ablations: Table 2 and the supplementary tables rigorously assess the contributions of individual elements, including instance-specific vs. fixed median schedule, frequency vs. power schedules, logSNR vs. t-based guidance intervals, and extra FiLM conditioning.

Novel controllable generation capability: Parameterizing the schedule via the power spectrum enables direct manipulation of image high-frequency detail/texture by scaling the power-law exponent (Figure 5).
weaknesses: Restricted experimental scope: The evaluation is confined strictly to class-conditional ImageNet generation. Testing on text-to-image datasets (e.g., MS-COCO) or general unstructured datasets would better substantiate the generality of the GMM-based RAPSD sampler.

Degradation at large step counts: As observed in Figure 3, FID slightly degrades when increasing NFE beyond an optimal threshold (e.g., at 512 steps), unlike standard diffusion models which typically plateau or monotonically improve with finer time discretizations. The authors note this phenomenon, but deeper theoretical or empirical insight into why this happens is missing.

Resolution-dependent guidance tuning remains: While the noise schedule itself automatically adapts across resolutions, the classifier-free guidance interval still requires empirical per-resolution re-tuning (Table 5), which partially offsets the claim of eliminating handcrafted adjustments across resolutions.

Computational overhead during training: The paper omits wall-clock measurements or discussions regarding the additional compute cost of computing per-image 2D FFTs and power-law least-squares fits during batch training.
